title: Introduction to Trigonometry
notes: Trigonometric ratios are defined for a right triangle relative to one of its acute angles: sin=opposite/hypotenuse, cos=adjacent/hypotenuse, tan=opposite/adjacent.
Reciprocal ratios: cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan. Also tan = sin/cos and cot = cos/sin.
As the angle increases from 0 to 90 degrees, sin increases from 0 to 1, cos decreases from 1 to 0, tan increases from 0 to undefined (infinity) at 90.
Ratios depend only on the angle, not on the triangle's size (similar triangles have equal ratios) -- this is the whole reason trig ratios are well-defined.

Specific angle values (0,30,45,60,90) must be memorized cold -- they're used constantly. Trick: sin values at 0,30,45,60,90 are root(0/4),root(1/4),root(2/4),root(3/4),root(4/4) = 0,1/2,1/root2,root3/2,1. cos is the same list reversed.
Trig ratios of complementary angles: sin(90-A)=cos A, cos(90-A)=sin A, tan(90-A)=cot A, cot(90-A)=tan A, sec(90-A)=cosec A, cosec(90-A)=sec A.
Three core Pythagorean identities (from Pythagoras theorem applied to a right triangle): sin^2A+cos^2A=1; 1+tan^2A=sec^2A (undefined at A=90); 1+cot^2A=cosec^2A (undefined at A=0).
Identity-proving strategy: convert everything to sin and cos first if stuck, simplify algebraically (common tricks: (1-sinA)(1+sinA)=cos^2A, multiply by conjugate, factor common terms).

examples.question: Express cos A, tan A and sec A in terms of sin A.
examples.solution: From sin^2A+cos^2A=1: cosA = root(1-sin^2A). Then tanA = sinA/root(1-sin^2A), secA = 1/root(1-sin^2A).
